obtained.how: the publisher's PDF (NRC Research Press) posted on the first author's lab website (Fish Ecology and Conservation Physiology Lab, Carleton University, fecpl.ca)

bibliography.note: Cooke, Philipp & Weatherhead, Can. J. Zool. 80: 756–770 (2002), title as cited; the issue (4) is from Crossref (the PDF does not print it).

claims.claim: by model, a 354–926-g smallmouth guarding for 22 days at 18 °C without food would lose 11.8–16.2 % of its mass
claims.location: p. 764 (PDF p. 9), Table 2; methods p. 760 (PDF p. 5)
claims.conditions: Fish Bioenergetics 3.0 with Rice (1981) smallmouth parameters; constant 18 °C; consumption set to 0; activity multiplier from each male's EMG-telemetry swimming speed by brood stage (egg 3 d, egg-sac fry 2, swim-up 2, free-swimming fry 15 = 22 d); six nesting males, Lake Opinicon, Ontario, 15 May–9 June 1998; wet mass
claims.note: The six smallmouth lost 11.8–16.2 % (larger fish proportionately less); the five largemouth 12.0–15.8 %. The no-food assumption is the authors' (from their unpublished video), which the paper rightly sets against Mackereth et al. 1999.

claims.claim: smallmouth nest guarding raises respiration +17.6 % averaged over the whole guard
claims.location: p. 763 (PDF p. 8), Results; p. 766 (PDF p. 11), Fig. 8
claims.quote: The specific respiration rate for a nesting 1000-g smallmouth bass was only 17.6% higher
claims.conditions: a modeled 1000-g fish at 18 °C over the 22-day simulation, nesting activity = the mean swimming speed over that period (Fig. 6); compared with non-nesting, fed Lake Erie smallmouth (0.317 m/s from the same transmitters)
claims.note: It is the specific respiration of a standard 1000-g fish, nesting vs non-nesting, over the monitored 22 days (not the whole ~28-day guard). Largemouth: 52.6 % higher. Activity of nesting fish was 'approximately double' that of non-nesting fish (abstract).

notes: Other values: a 1000-g nesting smallmouth would lose 115 g in 22 days (largemouth 125 g); a non-nesting one without food 98 g, and with 10 g/day of fish (4000 J/g) would gain 42 g (pp. 761 and 763, Fig. 7). Every guarding male had a negative growth rate and a mean daily energy loss above 10 000 J (p. 761, Table 2).
